metadata.title: Rollback the consensus module leader's uncommitted state

issue_payload.body:
This PR is to rollback the consensus module leader's uncommitted state in the case of an unexpected election.

In the cases of using control toggle for suspend, snapshot, shutdown, and resume - the consensus module leader updates its ConsensusModuleAgent#state. The corresponding cluster action added to the log is initially uncommitted. If an unexpected election occurs, the leader will need to rollback this uncommitted state to its committed value.

The leader's consensus module will track its previous states and log position corresponding to cluster action, while cluster action is uncommitted. For now, avoided using aeron-test-support TestCluster as using consensus module invoker for ease of testing and wanted to avoid making changes to TestCluster.

Feel free to close if I'm wrong, misunderstanding something, or there's a better approach.

issue_payload.body:
This fixes various things on Windows, and makes the CMake build and tests pass with VS 2019.

Every commit message explains the introduced changes in more detail.

discussion_timeline.author: mjpt777
discussion_timeline.body: [aeron-driver/src/main/c/aeron_windows.c] Why remove DllMain?

discussion_timeline.author: mjpt777
discussion_timeline.body: [aeron-driver/src/test/c/aeron_strutil_test.cpp] Why not keep the `aeron_free` version and have it do the right thing depending on platform?

discussion_timeline.author: ltrzesniewski
discussion_timeline.body:
[aeron-driver/src/main/c/aeron_windows.c] It does nothing useful, and wastes a TLS slot.

This code is basically taken from [the docs example](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/dlls/using-thread-local-storage-in-a-dynamic-link-library) but unlike the example it does not use `dwTlsIndex` anywhere outside of `DllMain`. So basically `DllMain` manages a TLS slot and some per-thread memory just for itself. The other TLS code does not need this.

discussion_timeline.author: ltrzesniewski
discussion_timeline.body:
[aeron-driver/src/test/c/aeron_strutil_test.cpp] `aeron_free` already does the right thing and calls `free`. I'm not sure why, but this additional indirection causes an assertion in the debug build. It looks like the two different modules use two different heaps.

In any case, I think `free` is more correct here, as the `strdup` docs tell you should call `free` on what it returns. Something like `aeron_free` could potentially switch to a different allocator in the future, breaking this code even for other platforms.

discussion_timeline.author: ltrzesniewski
discussion_timeline.body:
BTW would you accept a PR which adds a Windows CI, using something like GitHub Actions for instance (so it won't require you to setup any external account)?

If yes, would you like to also migrate the Linux CI from Travis to GitHub Actions for consistency?

discussion_timeline.body: Migrating to GitHub Actions is on my list of things to try. Travis has been very frustrating.

discussion_timeline.body: [aeron-driver/src/test/c/aeron_strutil_test.cpp] `aeron_free` should be used by all memory calls. The debug build is probably mixing new and malloc and not sorting it correctly.... or would be my best guess.

discussion_timeline.author: tmontgomery
discussion_timeline.body: [aeron-driver/src/main/c/aeron_windows.c] Actually, I think DllMain will be necessary. Currently, the error handling is broken in tests due to the TLS state not working. And that is partially due to it not being wired in correctly with DllMain or handling static libs correctly.

discussion_timeline.body: I've reverted so it can done in parts which are easily agreed.

discussion_timeline.author: tmontgomery
discussion_timeline.body: [aeron-driver/src/main/c/aeron_windows.c] A correct DllMain should use the existing slot and make the checks work. The changes to the TLS handling may work for static libs. Should write a test to make sure error handling is actually correct for threading, etc.

discussion_timeline.author: tmontgomery
discussion_timeline.body: Everything but the DllMain and the removal of aeron_free from the test are OK.

discussion_timeline.author: ltrzesniewski
discussion_timeline.body:
[aeron-driver/src/main/c/aeron_windows.c] I actually fixed the error handling in this PR, it was previously causing one of the unit tests to fail because `aeron_thread_once` was not working properly.

While we *could* make the TLS slot be managed by `DllMain`, it would break TLS if the media driver is used as a static library, since those don't use `DllMain`, and it would create the need to maintain different code paths for Windows and Linux.

I think the TLS code from this PR is fine, and it doesn't need a `DllMain` function to work properly, unless I'm misunderstanding something.

discussion_timeline.author: ltrzesniewski
discussion_timeline.body:
[aeron-driver/src/test/c/aeron_strutil_test.cpp] The code uses `strdup` so we can't really control how it allocates the memory. The docs simply say to use `free` to release it.
Under a MSVC debug build, going through `aeron_free` causes an assertion failure, while using `free` works fine.

discussion_timeline.author: tmontgomery
discussion_timeline.body:
[aeron-driver/src/main/c/aeron_windows.c] You don't need different code paths. The DllMain can just pre-populate the TLS key/slot. Same code in what is there now but with DllMain but thread once will need to see if the slot is pre-populate or not. And as you point out it is needed for static libs. 

A DllMain is needed as we have plans that do require it soon. Also, while it is small, it is an advantage to pre-populate on DLL attach when possible.

discussion_timeline.author: tmontgomery
discussion_timeline.body: [aeron-driver/src/test/c/aeron_strutil_test.cpp] As `aeron_free` uses free under the covers.... it indicates a different problem is at play. So, just moving to `free` does not fix that. Also, as I mentioned, all memory free should use `aeron_free`. Probably shouldn't be using `strdup` either. @mikeb01 can these not use `strdup` and be on the stack instead so that we can get rid of both `free` and `aeron_free` in this test?

discussion_timeline.author: tmontgomery
discussion_timeline.body: [aeron-driver/src/test/c/aeron_strutil_test.cpp] I've removed the strdup and free from the test as of 22401b35b

discussion_timeline.author: ltrzesniewski
discussion_timeline.body:
[aeron-driver/src/main/c/aeron_windows.c] > And as you point out it is needed for static libs.

Not exactly, I just said that `DllMain` is not called in static libs, which would require a different initialization path if you want to support them.

But since you have plans to require `DllMain` soon, I suppose that using the media driver as a static library will not be possible anymore in the future, right?

I could move the TLS slot handling to `DllMain` but my understanding is that it will make retrieving the error messages impossible in a static library on Windows as a consequence, unless we add the currently existing code in an `#if STATIC_LIBRARY` or something similar.

discussion_timeline.author: ltrzesniewski
discussion_timeline.body:
[aeron-driver/src/test/c/aeron_strutil_test.cpp] > can these not use `strdup` and be on the stack instead so that we can get rid of both `free` and `aeron_free` in this test?

I like that solution, it should be easy with a `strcpy` to the stack.

discussion_timeline.author: tmontgomery
discussion_timeline.body:
[aeron-driver/src/main/c/aeron_windows.c] This can be done, I think, quite easily. A static set to indicate that `TlsAlloc` has been called by DllMain means that `aeron_thread_key_create` doesn't need to call it. If not, then it can call `TlsAlloc`. All of this can be hidden in there. So, this shouldn't require anything weird. The use of `TlsSetValue` can still use the existing paths and created on demand.

If you are not comfortable about this or do not quite understand what I am suggesting. Just keep the DllMain and remove the TLS calls from it and keep the rest as you fixed it. I'll fix DllMain up when I have time.

In terms of requiring DllMain. Only the use of specific options may (or may not). Eventually, we would like to do DPDK, RIO, and other specific support. Some of that will be easier to integrate with DllMain than without.

discussion_timeline.author: tmontgomery
discussion_timeline.body: [aeron-driver/src/main/c/aeron_windows.c] BTW, in a static lib, won't the error state be a leak when the thread goes away? Meaning to avoid the leak, DLL would be a better idea? (I've not looked for a hook to catch thread death for a while)...

discussion_timeline.author: ltrzesniewski
discussion_timeline.body:
[aeron-driver/src/test/c/aeron_strutil_test.cpp] @tmontgomery OK I'm pretty sure I understand the problem now.

CMake generated different configurations regarding the CRT library for the media driver and the unit test: the media driver uses *"Multi-threaded Debug DLL (/MDd)"* while the test uses *"Multi-threaded Debug (/MTd)"*.

This basically means they use a different instance of the C runtime, so memory allocated by one cannot be freed by the other.

Anyway, your fix makes the issue go away.

discussion_timeline.author: tmontgomery
discussion_timeline.body: [aeron-driver/src/test/c/aeron_strutil_test.cpp] AH. Makes perfect sense. Glad you figured it out and mentioned it. And glad the change works. Thanks!

discussion_timeline.author: ltrzesniewski
discussion_timeline.body:
[aeron-driver/src/main/c/aeron_windows.c] Ok I think I understand what you're suggesting now. I'll implement that tomorrow.

> Eventually, we would like to do DPDK, RIO, and other specific support.

That's great! 👍

> Some of that will be easier to integrate with DllMain than without.

I figured an empty `DllMain` wouldn't be useful and you could add it back at a later time when needed. Anyway, I'll add it back with specific support for error messages.

> BTW, in a static lib, won't the error state be a leak when the thread goes away?

Yes, it will leak. That can be mitigated from `DllMain`. But if I understand correctly, it also means there's currently a leak on Linux.

discussion_timeline.body: [aeron-driver/src/main/c/aeron_windows.c] On Linux it doesn't leak because `pthread_key_create` takes `free` as the destructor arg. Which should be `aeron_free`, but sigh...

metadata.title: Added drain of queued commands during close to fix memory leaks

discussion_timeline.author: strangelydim
discussion_timeline.body: @vyazelenko hold off on this for just a bit... new test failure I need to address.

discussion_timeline.author: vyazelenko
discussion_timeline.body:
@strangelydim The existing approach assumed user's ownership of the `async` object's memory. Therefore application thread was responsible for freeing said memory by:
* Polling async object to completion.
* Cancelling async operation (new API added recently).
* Manually freeing async objects if no longer polling and/or aeron client is closed.

C++ Wrapper relies on this and does manual freeing once `Aeron` is closed, see:

https://github.com/aeron-io/aeron/blob/93e45901d06a32e490b536700e8244f0a8b411de/aeron-client/src/main/cpp_wrapper/Aeron.h#L91-L125

If we are going to change the existing logic than we need to update C++ Wrapper as well. 

I wonder what @mikeb01 thinks?

discussion_timeline.author: mikeb01
discussion_timeline.body:
The problem is if you have an cancel request inflight when the Aeron client is closed it will end up leaking because we have no other handle to that memory for a user to remove.

Another option would be to do something similar to the change I made in the driver, which was to use a ring buffer rather than a queue for the commands so that allocation is not required.  A command can just occupy space in the buffer.  For all of the add operations we would still need to allocate an object and for that store a pointer in the ring buffer, but for simple commands that don't need to be tracked by the user (e.g. cancels) the data can just be stored inline.

discussion_timeline.author: vyazelenko
discussion_timeline.body:
> The problem is if you have an cancel request inflight when the Aeron client is closed it will end up leaking because we have no other handle to that memory for a user to remove.

@mikeb01 You are right. I was thinking about the `async` stucts only but cancel requests are a problem.

The proposed approach will work, albeit not being the most efficient, since it will effectively execute all commands in the queue including create requests. The driver will remove all client-specific resources once the client is closed (provided a client can send a request to remove itself from the driver that is). 

The C++ Wrapper is effectively already using the same approach by calling `aeron_add_close_handler` which implicitly drains the command queue. So when the rest of the close proceeds there will be no commands in flight anymore.
_**NB:** All add/remove handler methods (e.g. `aeron_add_close_handler`, `aeron_remove_close_handler`, `aeron_add_available_counter_handler` etc.) are blocking and force command queue to drain in order to execute the request. Unlike the rest of the aeron client API which is asynchronous._

So the questions are:

1. Do we want to execute all pending commands or shall we just free the memory associated with them without executing?
   I'm inclined to simply free memory.

2. What shall we do with the `async` structs on close?
   Currently they are an end user responsibility. However, actual resources (e.g. `aeron_subscription_t`, `aeron_publication_t`) are freed in the close method. Therefore it seems sensible that the `async` structs in the `registering_resources` array should be also freed.

discussion_timeline.author: strangelydim
discussion_timeline.body:
OK, just pushed a new fix that I _think_ should work:

1. Keep track of all outstanding `aeron_client_remove_resource_cmd_t` objects in a list that is only ever modified by the user thread
2. Added a volatile `processed` flag to `aeron_client_remove_resource_cmd_t`, false initially, set to true by the conductor thread after it has gotten to the remove and handled it
3. `aeron_client_conductor_on_close` walks the list of outstanding `aeron_client_remove_resource_cmd_t` objects and frees all of them
4. To prevent that list from just accumulating and accumulating... it's also walked by `aeron_client_conductor_async_remove_resource`, but _only_ cmds that have already been processed are free'd and removed from the list.  But that should be good enough to keep the max size of the list fairly small in practice.

So... that's at least one possible approach.  Seems to work in my testing so far....

discussion_timeline.body:

But that should be good enough to keep the max size of the list fairly small in practice.
> 
>

I don't think it will work.

First of all, there could be multiple application threads using a single `aeron_client_t`, i.e. the client is thread safe and could be shared across multiple threads.

Second, there are at least two threads writing to that list: application thread (when submitting) and the conductor thread (when removing). So the list pointer access must be atomic and volatile. 

Why not simply scan command queue and free all instances of the `aeron_client_remove_resource_cmd_t`?

discussion_timeline.body:
> Ah nuts, didn't realize the client needed to be thread-safe... So nope, this won't work as-is.

Could band-aid it all even more and make the list of outstanding `aeron_client_remove_resource_cmd_t` objects thread-local, and have every user thread that calls `aeron_client_conductor_async_remove_resource` register a pointer to its thread-local outstanding `aeron_client_remove_resource_cmd_t` list to a master list o' lists (just on that thread's very first call to `aeron_client_conductor_async_remove_resource`) that is protected by an actual lock.

Each individual user thread would then be responsible for the "lazy" frees of its own remove_cmds that had already been processed, and the rest would then still be cleaned up by `aeron_client_conductor_on_close` which would walk through each of the thread-local lists at that point rather than just the one big list that's in my current commit.

Too complicated?

Seems to work great with pthreads... not so great on Windows, where the Aeron TLS code doesn't support TLS destructors. But could be modified to support them ala https://iangrunert.com/2025/08/04/fiber-local-storage-slow . Boy howdy, and I thought this would be simple.

discussion_timeline.author: vyazelenko
discussion_timeline.body:
> > OK, pushed yet another update to make this now one of the most complicated ways to ever fix a small and infrequent memory leak ever written... but... probably works and isn't slow?
> 
> Seems to work great with pthreads... not so great on Windows, where the Aeron TLS code doesn't support TLS destructors. But could be modified to support them ala https://iangrunert.com/2025/08/04/fiber-local-storage-slow . Boy howdy, and I thought this would be simple.

@strangelydim Can we step back and think about what problem we are trying to solve?

The main issue is pending `cancel` requests that were submitted but not yet executed by the client conductor thread, right? There is no problem if:
* `cancel` request failed during submission, i.e. no space in the conductor command queue in which case the request is freed on the application thread.
* `cancel` request was submitted and client conductor thread executed it. In this case the `cancel` struct will be freed on the conductor thread.

The remaining case is when such `cancel` request sits on the conductor command queue (`command_queue`). So how about we drain this queue in the `aeron_client_conductor_on_close` method and simply free every pending command? Similar to how we delete resources in the `resource_by_id_map` map. This would also solve the issue with non-polled `async` structs and will simplify our C++ Wrapper impl.

We use a similar approach when closing `async_executor`:

https://github.com/aeron-io/aeron/blob/a092f5bd9f04f882be4bc7cdec5a3e86c115edd5/aeron-client/src/main/c/concurrent/aeron_executor.c#L79-L93

/cc @mikeb01

discussion_timeline.author: strangelydim
discussion_timeline.body:
> So how about we drain this queue in the `aeron_client_conductor_on_close` method and simply free every pending command?

With or without calling the user's `on_complete` function?  We'd probably want to call it... presumably the user set it for a good reason it. Could that cause any issues?

discussion_timeline.author: vyazelenko
discussion_timeline.body:
> > So how about we drain this queue in the `aeron_client_conductor_on_close` method and simply free every pending command?
> 
> With or without calling the user's `on_complete` function? We'd probably want to call it... presumably the user set it for a good reason it. Could that cause any issues?

With `on_complete` function for parity with normal close operation. However, `_cancel` (e.g. `aeron_async_add_subscription_cancel`) and `_remove` (e.g. `aeron_async_remove_subscription`) APIs were added just 2 weeks ago (i.e. are not yet released) so we can change them not to have the `on_complete` functions. At the momemnt those are used to free the corresponding `async` struct.

discussion_timeline.author: strangelydim
discussion_timeline.body:
I really do think the `on_complete` callbacks are useful, and so wouldn't want to remove them, but also agree that the fancy TLS approach was overkill.

So new approach: tagged pointers. Set the LSB on remove cmds to mark them as such, and then we don't need to dereference each command in `aeron_client_conductor_on_close` to tell if it was a remove command or not (because if not, it was probably already free'd, so we'd blow up just trying to check what type of command it was). Now if the LSB is set, we know it's a remove command and safe to deref during close, calling the user's `on_complete` callback inline inside `aeron_client_conductor_on_close` and then free'ing the cmd.

No insane TLS machinery needed, preserves user callbacks and ordering, simple code.  @vyazelenko - just pushed to this branch if you'd like to take a look. I think this solution is fine as long as we can stomach using tagged pointers.  Tests all pass with this approach as well.

discussion_timeline.author: vyazelenko
discussion_timeline.body:
> Set the LSB on remove cmds to mark them as such, and then we don't need to dereference each command in aeron_client_conductor_on_close to tell if it was a remove command or not (because if not, it was probably already free'd, so we'd blow up just trying to check what type of command it was). 

When a command is processed it is removed from the list. So by definition the only items in the list are non-processed items and hence not yet freed.

To me the approach with pointer tagging seems like an overkill.

issue_payload.body:
This PR contains the following changes:
* Add `StorageSpaceException` that is thrown when there is not enough space to create a log buffer.
* Translate the above exception into the client visible error code `STORAGE_SPACE`.
* Update the C driver to return `AERON_ERROR_CODE_STORAGE_SPACE` if insufficient storage space when creating log buffers.
* [C] Fix storage space calculation on MacOS.
* [C] Add support for sparse files on Windows.
* [C] Allocate storage space for non-sparse files.
* [C] Recognize OS-specific out of disc space errors.
* [C] Add OS-specific error handling for the file system calls.

discussion_timeline.author: mikeb01
discussion_timeline.body:
It would be useful to have a system test, so that we can check that both the C driver and Java driver send the appropriate storage errors.  I think if we get a `AERON_ERROR_CODE_STORAGE_SPACE` I think it will come through as `AERON_ERROR_CODE_GENERIC_ERROR`.

I think the best would be to have the CI scripts create a tmpfs file system will a much smaller size (will need sudo access) such that it will trigger the error.  The test could have an assumption to check for the presence of that file system.  We'd only need to run it on Linux.

What would be also valuable is to print the `sessionId` of the replay Publication which is [encoded in the lower 32 bits](https://github.com/real-logic/aeron/blob/master/aeron-archive/src/main/java/io/aeron/archive/ArchiveConductor.java#L782) of the `replaySessionId`.

discussion_timeline.author: nbradac
discussion_timeline.body:
[aeron-agent/src/main/java/io/aeron/agent/ArchiveEventDissector.java] Oh I get it... if I use the &, the returned value is still a long, and the last bit is 0, so the number is positive.  If I cast to an int, it's an int... in which case (in the case of 20000000000), the last bit is a 1.  So the number is negative.  The 32 bits in question are the same, but how it looks when it gets printed is quite different.

Which is 'correct'?  Seems like in most places the session id is passed around as a long, in which case casting to an int and printing that is probably the wrong approach.

discussion_timeline.author: vyazelenko
discussion_timeline.body:
[aeron-agent/src/main/java/io/aeron/agent/ArchiveEventDissector.java] `Publication#sessionId` is a 32 bit value (`int` in Java) so casting to an `int` is correct way to extract this value out of `long` value.
Running this test:
```java
@ParameterizedTest
    @ValueSource(ints = { Integer.MIN_VALUE, -777, -1, 0, 1, 42, Integer.MAX_VALUE })
    void extractSessionId(final int sessionId)
    {
        final int replayId = 0xFF;
        final long replicationSessionId = ((long)replayId << 32) | (sessionId & 0xFFFF_FFFFL);
        System.out.println("replicationSessionId=" + replicationSessionId);
        System.out.println("cast: " + (int)replicationSessionId);
        System.out.println("mask: " + (replicationSessionId & 0xFFFF_FFFFL));
    }
```

